news.title: New civic agreement promises a fresh start for local communities
news.metaDescription: Leaders say the cross-community package will put neighbourhood priorities at the centre of public investment.
news.excerpt: Leaders say the cross-community package will put neighbourhood priorities at the centre of public investment.
news.imageAlt: New civic agreement promises a fresh start for local communities
takeaways: The agreement creates a five-year community renewal fund.
Local panels will help decide which projects move first.
The first funding round is expected to open this autumn.

content.text: A new chapter

A new civic agreement has set out a five-year plan to revive high streets, improve public spaces and support local services. The package brings together councils, community organisations and business groups around a shared set of priorities.
Supporters described the plan as practical and measurable, with quarterly progress reports promised from the outset.
Supporters described the plan as practical and measurable, with quarterly progress reports promised from the outset.
What changes first
The first projects will focus on safer walking routes, vacant buildings and small grants for neighbourhood groups. Each district will publish a shortlist before final decisions are made.

content.alt: New civic agreement promises a fresh start for local communities
content.caption: Reporting from The Northern Journal newsroom.

content.text: Officials said the process was designed to make local knowledge visible in funding decisions rather than treating consultation as an afterthought.
Community reaction
Residents welcomed the emphasis on visible improvements but said delivery would be the real test. Several groups called for clear timelines and accessible public reporting.
The first public meetings are due to begin next month, with project applications expected to follow in the autumn.

news.metaTitle: US-Iran Strait of Hormuz Clash: Control After Strikes
news.title: US-Iran Strait of Hormuz Clash: Control After Strikes
news.metaDescription: US and Iran exchanged strikes over the Strait of Hormuz, each claiming control as diplomacy continues and fears of wider regional conflict grow.
news.excerpt: A growing US-Iran clash over the Strait of Hormuz has intensified after weekend strikes, with both sides claiming control while diplomacy remains in the balance. The escalating conflict threatens regional security and raises fears of a wider Middle East war.
news.imageAlt: Naval vessels patrol near the Strait of Hormuz amid rising US-Iran tensions.

content.text: A dangerous standoff over one of the world's most important shipping corridors deepened over the weekend, with both Washington and Tehran declaring they hold control of the Strait of Hormuz after a fresh round of strikes rippled across the Middle East. The exchange has cast fresh doubt on efforts to keep a fragile truce framework alive, just as it approaches its midpoint.

The latest flashpoint began when Iranian forces struck a container vessel moving through the strait near Oman's coastline. The narrow passage at the mouth of the Persian Gulf has long carried a huge share of the world's crude oil and natural gas exports, and shipping through it has been disrupted repeatedly since fighting broke out, as Iranian forces have targeted commercial vessels to pressure international shippers.
A Truce on Shaky Ground

The two countries are roughly halfway through a 60-day interim arrangement that was intended to pave the way toward a lasting settlement. Instead, that window has been marked by repeated strikes centered on the strait and who gets to control it. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that slipping back into all-out fighting would carry devastating costs for the region and beyond.

US Central Command said its forces struck dozens of Iranian sites, including radar installations, air-defense batteries, missile and drone infrastructure, and small vessels, insisting the waterway remains a global trade artery that Iran does not control. European officials echoed that position, with the EU's top diplomat calling for shipping through the strait to return to normal, pre-war conditions.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard, which oversees the country's ballistic missile program and remains one of its most powerful institutions, pushed back forcefully, framing the waterway as sovereign Iranian territory and casting the American presence there as unwelcome foreign interference.
Strikes Spread Across the Region

The fallout was felt well beyond Iranian and American forces directly involved. Air-raid sirens sounded multiple times in Bahrain, home to the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, while Kuwait reported intercepting incoming fire. Jordan's military said it shot down several Iranian missiles without any casualties or damage, despite hosting American troops and aircraft of its own.

Inside Iran, state media reported strikes and at least two deaths across several provinces, including Hormozgan and Khuzestan, with additional reports of attacks further east. Oman, which has often served as a go-between for Tehran and Western governments, formally protested to an Iranian diplomat over the strike on the container ship in its waters.

A separate drone strike also hit a base linked to an Iranian Kurdish opposition faction operating from northern Iraq, though no group has claimed responsibility and details on casualties remain unclear.
Oil Markets and Diplomacy in the Balance

Iran's grip on the strait triggered a spike in global energy prices earlier in the conflict, though crude has since eased well off its wartime peak near $120 a barrel. Tehran's foreign ministry placed blame for the region's instability squarely on Washington, arguing that earlier understandings between the two sides had effectively collapsed. Iranian officials also signaled they would continue barring international inspectors from nuclear sites hit by US strikes last year, where a significant stockpile of enriched uranium is believed to remain.

Despite the harsh rhetoric, back-channel diplomacy has not stopped entirely. Mediators from Pakistan, Qatar and Egypt have continued pushing for a durable agreement, and Pakistan's foreign minister held direct talks with his Iranian counterpart urging both sides to step back from further escalation.

Adding another layer of uncertainty, Iran's newly installed supreme leader, who has stayed out of public view since the war began, issued his first statement since his predecessor's funeral, vowing retaliation. With strikes continuing and mediation efforts fragile, analysts say the coming weeks will likely determine whether the region edges toward a wider war or finds its way back to the negotiating table.
